sections.heading: What being technical looks like hands-off
sections.content: It means knowing what is going on and paying attention—not necessarily choosing the tools for the team. A leader should understand the work well enough to ask good questions, help guide decisions, listen, and ask about plans and major technical challenges. Fournier cautions that senior leaders who have been hands-off can lose credibility by dictating choices such as which library to use.

sections.heading: How to maintain technical credibility
sections.content: Fournier recommends surrounding yourself with smart technical people, listening to them discuss technology, asking questions, and staying interested in their problems—including detailed issues like debugging a database. Keeping close to a network of people who remain hands-on helps maintain technical savvy and credibility, even when you are not writing code yourself.

sections.heading: Why prior hands-on mastery matters
sections.content: She advises not stopping hands-on technical work until you have developed a durable baseline mastery—enough that after time away you might be rusty or slower, but would regain skill relatively quickly rather than be clueless. That experience can preserve confidence in your technical know-how and empathy for what good engineering involves.

answer.summary: For Camille Fournier, a hands-off leader stays technical by building real hands-on mastery first, then remaining informed, curious, and able to guide engineers with thoughtful questions rather than prescribing specific tools.

sections.heading: Build a foundation before stepping back
sections.content: Fournier advises not stopping hands-on technical work until you have a durable baseline mastery—enough that, even after becoming rusty, you could regain your skills relatively quickly. That foundation supports confidence in your technical judgment and empathy for what good engineering involves. She describes her own path as an undergraduate and graduate education plus four or five years of full-time work, and estimates roughly 10 years of substantial coding experience as a possible heuristic, not a strict rule.

sections.heading: Stay engaged without dictating implementation
sections.content: Being technical as a hands-off leader means knowing what is going on, paying attention, and understanding the work well enough to ask good questions and help the team reach better decisions. Rather than telling engineers which library to use, ask what they have considered, how they plan to handle a situation, and what the major implementation challenges are; then listen thoughtfully to their answers.

sections.heading: Keep learning from hands-on engineers
sections.content: She recommends surrounding yourself with smart technical people, listening to them discuss technology, and asking questions—including about concrete problems such as debugging a database issue. Maintaining contact with people who are still hands-on helps her stay technically savvy and credible, even though she is not writing code.
